label: GPT-6.1 Sol
output:
Jess, I know what you meant.

When you texted me last night that this was one assignment and I shouldn’t torch my job over it, I didn’t hear you saying the history didn’t matter. I heard a friend who knows what schools can do to teachers asking whether I’d thought through what might happen next.

I have. Or I’m trying to. That’s partly why I’m writing this instead of continuing to make the group chat unbearable.

For anybody who missed the beginning: for the last four years, my US History II juniors have done an oral history project about Boston’s busing and school desegregation crisis in 1974–76. They interview somebody in their family or neighborhood, make a ten-minute recording, and write a two-page reflection. I teach two sections, so we end up with a small, very uneven collection of memories: things people witnessed, things they heard about, things they’ve spent fifty years explaining to themselves.

This year, a parent emailed Dr. Halvorsen and copied a school committee member. She said the assignment “reopens wounds” and “pressures kids to judge their grandparents.” Halvorsen wants me to quietly drop it. We’re meeting with the parent on Thursday, November 19, at 3:15.

I’m planning to go into that meeting with a revised assignment, not an announcement that I’ve canceled it.

And before this becomes a story about a righteous history teacher standing up to a terrible parent: I think she has a point.

Asking a teenager to interview a relative sounds straightforward when you type it into an assignment sheet. It isn’t necessarily straightforward at the kitchen table. There are family rules about what you ask, who gets to ask it, and what happens if you don’t accept the first answer. A kid may be perfectly comfortable challenging me in class and completely unable to say, “Grandpa, can you tell me more about that?”

Also, “my teacher said I have to” is pressure, even if I didn’t intend it that way. I can’t pretend otherwise just because I like the work students have produced.

So I’m adding another route. Students will be able to interview a librarian or archivist, or work with recordings from previous years where we have permission to use them. Nobody will have to interview a family member. The assignment needs to make that choice real, not tuck it into a sentence that makes the alternative sound like the lesser version.

That’s a change I should have made before somebody complained.

But I don’t think the next step is to stop teaching this history through the voices of people who lived it.

In 2023, a student interviewed his grandmother, who had driven a school bus in South Boston in 1974. She had never told anyone in the family about it. He played about forty seconds of the recording for the class.

Then nobody said anything for what felt like a full minute.

I’m leaving out details here because a student’s family story isn’t automatically mine to publish. But I remember that silence. Usually, after a recording, I have to manage the transition: stop a side conversation, ask somebody to put a phone away, get us back to the questions. That day I didn’t have to do any of it.

I don’t know what every kid was thinking. I’m not going to turn a quiet classroom into proof that I changed thirty lives. What I know is that they were listening to somebody’s grandmother talk about a part of her life her own family hadn’t known about. For a little while, nobody seemed in a hurry to move on.

Last year, another student learned that her uncle had thrown rocks at a bus. She was upset. We talked after class twice. Her reflection was the best thing I read all year.

I hesitate even to put those two sentences next to each other, because they can make her distress sound like the price of getting a good paper. It wasn’t. If she’d needed to stop, she should have been able to stop. A grade doesn’t entitle me to push a kid through a family revelation.

What was good about her reflection was the care she took with something she couldn’t easily resolve. She was trying to understand what her uncle had done and what it meant to know that about someone in her family. She didn’t owe me a neat conclusion, and she didn’t write one.

That is work worth making room for. It also needs limits.

I catch myself thinking that the kids who are most uncomfortable with this history are the ones who need it most. Sometimes I think that’s true. I also know how convenient that belief can be for a teacher. Once I decide discomfort proves the lesson is working, I can explain away almost anything a student tells me.

I don’t get to do that. I don’t get to force an interview, demand a disclosure, or decide how much strain somebody else’s family can bear. I do get to ask students to study what happened here, look closely at evidence, and think about the accounts people give of their own lives. I need an assignment that lets them do that without making access to a relative—or willingness to question one—a requirement.

Because this is the history of the city they live in. The textbook gives it one paragraph.

A paragraph can tell them that desegregation happened and that people resisted it. It can’t do much with the memories still sitting in their neighborhoods, or with the fact that people they know may have been children on those buses, parents waiting for them, drivers, protesters, or people who stayed home and watched the news. Those are worth asking about carefully. Not every student has to be the person who asks.

And yes, Jess, I could still get burned.

I’ve had tenure since 2021. That matters, and I shouldn’t talk as if I have no protection. But Halvorsen controls my schedule and who gets AP classes. There are plenty of ways for this to make my working life worse without anybody firing me.

You know that. We met student teaching in 2012; you’ve known me long enough to recognize when I’m getting attached to being right. You also spent enough years in schools before leaving in 2019 to know that a reasonable explanation doesn’t guarantee a reasonable outcome.

I’m a little scared. I’d prefer to be writing about a successful project after the fact, with the meeting safely behind me. I don’t particularly want to sit in that office and disagree with my principal.

But I can’t find a good reason to cancel the whole assignment when the strongest objection to it is something I can address. The parent is worried about pressure on kids. I want to take that seriously and show her what I’m changing. I’m not going in to defeat her. I hope we can leave with an assignment she can see her child having a genuine choice within.

You don’t have to agree that keeping it is worth the risk. I know your text came from caring about me, and I’m glad you sent it, even if my response has now exceeded any reasonable definition of a text back.

I just wanted you to know what I’m trying to keep, and what I’m willing to change.

I’ll text you Thursday after the meeting. You can still tell me I’m being an idiot. I’d rather hear it from you.
